traveler: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah al-Ghafiqi
title: The Tihamah to the Pavement of the Martyrs: the Wali of al-Andalus and the Farthest Ride North
years: birth year unrecorded - 732 (the documented life runs 721-732)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Tihamah and the Road West

stops.name: Tihamah, born to the tribe of Ghafiq
stops.date_confidence: unrecorded. No chronicle gives a birth year; the date shown is a placeholder generated from his 721 seniority and carries no authority. The place is disputed inside the Arabic tradition itself: English Wikipedia has the Ghafiq in the Tihamah of Arabia, Arabic Wikipedia puts his birth in the Hijaz and files the Ghafiq under the tribe of Akk. The coordinate is a generic point in the Tihamah lowland and deliberately names no settlement.
stops.campa: No chronicle records the year, and the tribe's own genealogists disagree about the ground. One tradition places the Banu Ghafiq in the Tihamah, the hot coastal lowland along the Red Sea; the other puts his birth in the Hijaz. A boy is born to Abd Allah of the Ghafiq somewhere inside that argument. Nothing else of the first decades survives: no teacher, no first campaign, no marriage, no face. The record of Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi opens when he is already a soldier in another man's army, on the far side of a continent.
suggested_refs: The Tihamah coastal lowland along the Red Sea, tribal country of the Banu Ghafiq
sources: Arabic Wikipedia, entry on al-Ghafiqi (Hijaz; Ghafiq of Akk)
Later Arabic genealogical tradition as preserved in Ibn Idhari and al-Maqqari, both centuries after the subject

stops.name: Kairouan, the tribe in Ifriqiya
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The date is a placeholder inside the early eighth century. No source places al-Ghafiqi personally in Kairouan or fixes when he passed through the Maghreb; the milieu is assigned to him by biographers writing generations later.
stops.campa: The Arab tribes move west behind the armies, and Kairouan is where the Maghreb is governed and taught. Al-Ghafiqi is placed in this milieu by biographers writing long after him; not one of them says when he came, or whether he prayed in the great mosque, or what he did there. What the tradition does report is that he becomes known to Musa ibn Nusayr and to Musa's son Abd al-Aziz. A generation before him, these same Umayyad armies broke Dihya in the Aures and sent her head to the caliph at Damascus. This province is what that conquest made.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Kairouan, administrative and religious centre of Umayyad Ifriqiya
sources: Ibn Idhari, Al-Bayan al-Mughrib, on Arab tribal settlement in Ifriqiya (not a specific attestation of al-Ghafiqi)
dihya.journey.json, for the Umayyad conquest chain that produced the province

stops.name: Ceuta, the crossing of the strait
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No chronicle names his crossing, the year, the ship, or the company. The only fixed point is that he is in the peninsula by 721. The pool's original pin at Tangier is discarded: the conquest crossings ran Ceuta to Gibraltar and Tarifa across the narrows, not from Tangier down the Atlantic coast.
stops.campa: The strait is nine miles of water and the whole conquest passes over it. No chronicle names the ship that carried al-Ghafiqi, or the month, or the men he rode with. He is on the far shore by 721, ranking high enough in the governor's army to survive its destruction and be remembered for surviving it. The crossing is reconstructed backward from that one fact and from the route every other column used: Ceuta to the rock, the narrows rather than the long water from Tangier. He goes over as one name among thousands and lands in a province five years old.
suggested_refs: The strait of Gibraltar at its narrowest, the Ceuta crossing used by the conquest columns from 711
sources: Inference from Ibn Idhari's account of Al-Samh's 721 campaign, in which al-Ghafiqi appears as a ranking officer
No chronicle names the crossing: recorded as a gap

stops.name: Cordoba, the seat of the wali
stops.date_confidence: attested for the city, reconstruction for the man. Cordoba as seat of the wali under Al-Samh ibn Malik is well attested. That al-Ghafiqi held rank there, or mustered with the army in this city, is not: no chronicle records his rank or station before 721.
stops.campa: Cordoba governs al-Andalus for the caliph in Damascus, and Al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani holds it. Al-Ghafiqi serves under him. That is the whole of what is attested about his standing before Toulouse: no rank, no office, no command named. A century later this same city will hold Ziryab's lute and set the table manners of Europe; four centuries on, Maimonides will be born in it, and Ibn Arabi will meet Ibn Rushd inside its walls. In 721 it is a garrison capital with a frontier eight hundred miles long and an army going north.
suggested_refs: Cordoba, capital of Umayyad al-Andalus under the walis, before the emirate
sources: Chronicle of 754 (Continuatio Hispana), on Cordoba as seat of Umayyad government
ziryab.journey.json, maimonides.journey.json, ibn_arabi.journey.json, for the inherited Cordoba pin

stops.name: Narbonne, the forward base in Gaul
stops.date_confidence: attested for the garrison, inferred for the month. Narbonne is Umayyad from 719 and is the forward base for the Aquitaine campaign; the precise date the column marched out is not recorded.
stops.campa: Narbonne has been Umayyad since 719, the one city of Gaul the caliphate holds outright, and Al-Samh's army goes north from here. Septimania is a caliphal province now, and the coastal road and the Aude valley answer to Cordoba. The gate opens onto the road to Toulouse, which is Duke Odo's, and Al-Samh means to have it. Al-Ghafiqi rides in that column. No source places him anywhere in particular within it, names the man at his shoulder, or counts the men riding under him.
suggested_refs: Narbonne, capital of Umayyad Septimania from 719
sources: Ibn Idhari, Al-Bayan al-Mughrib, on Narbonne as the Umayyad foothold in Gaul
charles_martel.journey.json, for the inherited Narbonne pin

stops.name: Toulouse, the siege broken by Odo
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Chronicle of 754 and the Arabic tradition agree on the defeat and on Al-Samh's mortal wound. Al-Ghafiqi's presence is attested only as an escape: English Wikipedia places him among those who managed to get away. His rank and role during the campaign are nowhere stated and are inferred backward from his later prominence.
stops.campa: The army sits before Toulouse and does not take it. Then Odo of Aquitaine comes back with the levies of the south and falls on the siege lines from outside. The Umayyad camp breaks. Al-Samh takes a mortal wound and much of the officer corps dies on the field. Al-Ghafiqi is among those who get out alive, which is the first thing any source records about him and the only reason there is a later career to record. Two hundred and thirteen years before this, Clovis rode into this city for the treasure of Alaric.
suggested_refs: The field before Toulouse, 9 June 721, where Odo relieved the siege
sources: clovis.journey.json, for the inherited Toulouse pin

stops.name: Narbonne, the death of Al-Samh
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death, reconstruction for al-Ghafiqi's part in the withdrawal. The Arabic tradition gives him charge of the retreat; modern historians read that as probable rather than proven. The month is inferred from the 9 June battle.
stops.campa: They carry the governor back down the road to Narbonne and he dies there of the wound. The army that took Barcelona and Narbonne in two seasons is now a column of survivors inside a garrison town with no commander. The Arabic tradition hands the withdrawal into Septimania and onward toward the passes to al-Ghafiqi, and it is a plausible hand to put it in, since he is the senior man who came back. The chronicles themselves say only that Al-Samh died and that the army went home.
suggested_refs: Narbonne, where Al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani died of his Toulouse wound
sources: charles_martel.journey.json, for the inherited Narbonne pin

stops.name: Cordoba, the interim command
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact, corrected for the length. The pool gave 721-722 and 'roughly a year'; Al-Samh died 9 June 721 and Anbasa was appointed later the same year, so the interim ran a matter of months in 721. The exact month of the handover is not recorded.
stops.campa: The province needs a governor before Damascus can name one, and the men who came back from Toulouse put forward the officer who brought them back. Al-Ghafiqi holds al-Andalus as acting wali. It is his first time in the seat and it lasts months rather than the year the later genealogies round it up to: Al-Samh dies in June and the caliph's appointee is in place before the year turns. He governs a province that has just lost an army and a governor in the same week, and he governs it on borrowed authority.
suggested_refs: The succession lists of the walis of al-Andalus, in which the 721 interim appears without a caliphal appointment
sources: Akhbar Majmu'a, on the sequence of governors in the 720s

stops.name: Cordoba, Anbasa takes the seat
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, inferred for the month. English Wikipedia dates Anbasa's appointment to 721, not 722; the pool's 722 is corrected here. No source gives the day or month.
stops.campa: Anbasa ibn Suhaym al-Kalbi arrives with the appointment and the interim ends. Al-Ghafiqi steps down without incident. The governorship of al-Andalus turns over again and again through this decade, and few who leave it leave it upright. He is given a command in the east of the peninsula instead, and the record closes over him. It does not open again for nine years. Whatever he thought about being passed over for the seat he had just held, no chronicler asked and no chronicler guessed.
suggested_refs: The succession of walis of al-Andalus, 721 to 730

stops.name: Zaragoza, the eastern command
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The sources say only that he was given command in eastern al-Andalus. No chronicle names Zaragoza, the year, or one thing he did there. The date is a placeholder at the start of the gap.
stops.campa: Eastern al-Andalus is what the sources say, and eastern al-Andalus is governed from the Ebro. Zaragoza is the inference, not the attestation. No chronicle names the city, the year, or a single action of his in it. Nine years run between his two governorships and no source puts anything at all into them. Berber garrisons are restive across the Maghreb and the northern marches through this decade, and he is somewhere inside that, holding a frontier for a caliph he has never met and will never meet.
suggested_refs: The Upper March of al-Andalus, governed from Zaragoza on the Ebro
sources: Wikipedia, 'Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi' (eastern command, no city named)
Recorded as a documented gap: 722 to 730 is blank in every source consulted

stops.name: Narbonne, Anbasa does not come home
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, contested for the manner, inferred for the place. English Wikipedia states Anbasa died of natural causes in 726 during his campaign in Aquitaine; some Arabic traditions have him mortally wounded in a rearguard action during the retreat. The two versions are flagged, not merged. The pin is his Septimanian base, not a recorded death site.
stops.campa: Anbasa carries the war back into Aquitaine and does not return from it. One account has him dying of natural causes in the middle of the campaign; another has him mortally wounded covering the retreat. The record does not choose and neither does this stop. After him a run of short tenures follows in Cordoba, governor after governor, and the frontier that Al-Samh pushed to Toulouse and Anbasa pushed up the Rhone stops moving north. Al-Ghafiqi is not in any of these years. He is in the east, out of the light.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad campaigns up the Rhone valley, 725 to 726, and their collapse after Anbasa
sources: Arabic tradition of a mortal wound in the retreat, flagged as contradictory
charles_martel.journey.json, for the inherited Narbonne pin

stops.name: Damascus, the caliph names him
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment and the year, inferred for the month. The sources credit Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik with the choice; whether the order in fact came from Damascus or from the Ifriqiyan seat at Kairouan is not settled by the sources consulted here.
stops.campa: Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik rules from Damascus, and the sources say the caliph himself names al-Ghafiqi to al-Andalus a second time: intelligent, eloquent, a capable administrator. That is the whole character sketch the record allows him, three adjectives in a chancery hand. Damascus is where Dihya's head was carried a generation earlier, tribute from the last Berber resistance in the Aures. The city takes in heads and sends out governors. Al-Andalus is months of road away and it receives its wali by letter.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad caliphal chancery at Damascus under Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, 724 to 743
sources: dihya.journey.json ('Damascus, the head before the Caliph'), for the inherited Damascus pin

stops.name: Cordoba, wali a second time
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, inferred for the month. The pool gave the Cerdanya suppression as the qualification for this appointment; that is chronologically impossible, since the revolt is dated 731, after the appointment. The causal claim is removed here.
stops.campa: He takes the seat he held for a few months nine years ago, and this time it is his for two and a half years. The province he inherits is quarrelsome and its frontier has not moved since Toulouse. What he does with the administration goes unrecorded; what he does with the army fills every chronicle that mentions his name. The appointment is dated 730. The deed later offered as his qualification for it, the breaking of the Cerdanya revolt, will not happen until 731.
suggested_refs: The second governorship of al-Andalus, 730 to 732

stops.name: Cerdanya, the marriage that made a lordship
stops.date_confidence: attested for the alliance and the marriage, traditional for the site, inferred for the month. Neither the Chronicle of 754 nor the Fredegar continuator names the fortress; Llivia is the traditional identification and the coordinate follows it.
stops.campa: Uthman ibn Naissa governs the Pyrenean marches for Cordoba. The Franks call him Munuza. He makes his own peace with Odo of Aquitaine and seals it by marrying Odo's daughter, and the frontier valley of the Cerdanya becomes a lordship answering to neither Cordoba nor Toulouse. It is the one arrangement in this whole story where the two sides of the mountains agree about anything. It lasts a year. Odo has bought a shield across the passes and he is about to watch it taken away.
suggested_refs: Llivia in the Cerdanya, traditional seat of the lordship of Uthman ibn Naissa

stops.name: Cerdanya, the revolt put down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the suppression and the year, contradictory for the death. The Chronicle of 754 has Uthman killed in the fighting; later Arabic tradition has him die by his own hand rather than be captured. The two traditions are recorded and not reconciled. The month is not given.
stops.campa: Al-Ghafiqi marches into the valley and the breakaway lordship ends. How Uthman ends is disputed and stays disputed: the Latin chronicle has him killed in the fighting, the later Arabic tradition has him go off a cliff rather than be taken alive. Both agree the frontier returns to Cordoba's hand. Odo has now lost his one ally south of the mountains, and the man who took that ally away has the whole Pyrenean line at his back and no reason left to stay behind it.
suggested_refs: The Cerdanya, the Pyrenean valley straddling the frontier between al-Andalus and Aquitaine
sources: Chronicle of 754 (Continuatio Hispana), on death in the fighting
Ibn Idhari, Al-Bayan al-Mughrib, and al-Maqqari, Nafh al-Tib, on the fall from the cliff
Wikipedia, 'Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi', which notes the contradiction explicitly

stops.name: Cordoba, the province called to arms
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and internally contested. One strand of the pool placed the muster at Cordoba and cited the Chronicle of 754 for it; the chronicle contains no Cordoba mustering scene, and the biography article says the wali assembled troops in Pamplona. This stop is kept as the summons and demoted to reconstruction; the muster itself is pinned at Pamplona.
stops.campa: The order goes out across al-Andalus and the contingents come in: Arab heavy horse, Berber light horse, troops drawn from other provinces of the caliphate. Some accounts have recruits called from Yemen and the Levant, a detail modern historians mark dubious. Where the host actually forms up is disputed inside the record: one strand assembles it here in the capital, and the article that carries his biography says plainly that the wali assembled troops in Pamplona. Both readings are kept and neither is adjudicated.
suggested_refs: The provincial levy of al-Andalus, 732, Arab and Berber contingents with troops from other caliphal provinces
sources: New World Encyclopedia, 'Battle of Tours', on the composition of the army
Wikipedia, 'Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi', on Pamplona as the muster point
Chronicle of 754: contains no Cordoba muster, contra the pool's citation

stops.name: Pamplona, the host assembled
stops.date_confidence: attested for the place, inferred for the month. English Wikipedia states the wali assembled troops in Pamplona. The season is reconstructed from the campaign's later dates.
stops.campa: Pamplona is where the host comes together, in the basin the western passes open onto. How many men is unknowable: modern estimates run from twenty thousand to eighty thousand, and the medieval figures are worse than useless, one chronicle claiming three hundred and seventy-five thousand Muslim dead at the end of it. With the army travel its camp followers, its wives, its concubines, and, shortly, the plunder of Aquitaine. Forty-six years from now Charlemagne will have these gates opened for him and will raze the walls on his way home.
stops.quote: And that army went through all places like a desolating storm.
stops.quote_source: Anonymous Arab chronicler, as rendered by Edward Shepherd Creasy, The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World, ch. 7, following Jose Antonio Conde, Historia de la Dominacion de los Arabes en Espana (Madrid, 1820); text at Fordham, Internet Medieval Sourcebook. A nineteenth-century Romantic rendering of the Arabic tradition, not a primary chronicle speaking in its own voice.
suggested_refs: Pamplona, muster point of the 732 army
Creasy's chapter on Tours, the channel through which Conde's Arabic sources reached English
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours', on the disputed troop numbers and the 375,000 casualty figure
charlemagne.journey.json, for the inherited Pamplona pin

stops.name: Roncesvalles, over the Pyrenees
stops.date_confidence: attested for the crossing, reconstruction for the pass and the month. Primary sources state only that the army crossed the Pyrenees. Roncesvalles is a traditional identification; other western passes remain possible.
stops.campa: The column crosses. No eighth-century source names the pass, and Roncesvalles is the traditional identification rather than an attested one; other western crossings remain open. What is attested is the crossing and what lies on the far side of it, which is Gascony, then Aquitaine, then a duke who broke this same army eleven years ago at Toulouse. Charlemagne's rearguard will die in this defile in 778 and be sung about for four hundred years. Nobody will ever write a song about this crossing from the side that made it.
stops.quote: Then Abderrahman, [the Muslim emir] seeing the land filled with the multitude of his army, crossed the Pyrenees, and traversed the defiles [in the mountains] and the plains, so that he penetrated ravaging and slaying clear into the lands of the Franks.
stops.quote_source: Isidore of Beja's Chronicle (the Continuation of the Chronicle of 754), trans. William Stearns Davis, Readings in Ancient History, vol. 2; Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks Project
suggested_refs: The pass of Roncesvalles, traditional crossing of the 732 army and site of the 778 ambush

stops.name: Bordeaux, Odo broken before the city
stops.date_confidence: attested for the defeat, inferred for the day. The atlas date is inherited from charles_martel.journey.json, which pins Bordeaux and the Garonne together at 732-06-15; no source gives a day.
stops.campa: Odo of Aquitaine meets him outside Bordeaux with what he has and is beaten in the field. It is Toulouse reversed, fought eleven years later by one of the officers who ran from Toulouse, and no chronicle on either side remarks on the symmetry. The duke gets away south with the remnant of his levy. The city does not get away. It stands undefended behind him, and in front of it is an army that has crossed a mountain range, ridden the length of Gascony, and not yet been paid for either.
suggested_refs: Bordeaux, where Odo of Aquitaine was defeated in the field in 732
sources: charles_martel.journey.json, for the inherited Bordeaux pin

stops.name: Bordeaux, the sack
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sack, inferred for the day. The sequence is corrected against the pool, which had the sack following the Garonne: Wikipedia's 'Battle of the River Garonne' states the Garonne engagement came after the victory at Bordeaux.
stops.campa: The army takes Bordeaux and burns it. Palaces come down, churches burn, and the Frankish continuator of Fredegar writes the devastation up in the worst terms he has. Neither he nor the Chronicle of 754 says which churches. To the people in its path this is no longer a raid on the marches; it is a conquest, and Aquitaine is inside it. Two hundred and twenty-five years before, Clovis wintered in this city after Vouille and took Aquitaine off the Goths.
suggested_refs: The sack of Bordeaux, summer 732

stops.name: Bordeaux, the basilica of Saint-Seurin
stops.date_confidence: tradition. Local ecclesiastical tradition at Bordeaux counts Saint-Seurin among the churches burned. No contemporary source names it or any other church by name; the chroniclers report burned churches and leave the list open.
stops.campa: The basilica of Saint-Seurin stands outside the old walls and is already ancient in 732, a burial church venerated for three centuries. Bordeaux tradition counts it among the buildings that burned. No contemporary source names it, or any other church; the chroniclers report burned churches and let whoever wants a list supply one. Bordeaux supplied Saint-Seurin. The tradition is recorded here as tradition, and what it remembers is that the fire took the holy places first and the oldest of them soonest.
suggested_refs: The basilica of Saint-Seurin, Bordeaux, an early Christian burial church standing in 732
sources: Not named in the Chronicle of 754 or the Fredegar continuations: recorded as unattested

stops.name: The Garonne, Odo's second army destroyed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle, reconstruction for the site and the day. Wikipedia's 'Battle of the River Garonne' locates the engagement at Bordeaux, 45 degrees 02 minutes 29 seconds N, 0 degrees 36 minutes 24 seconds W. The pool's 44.6, 0.2 is discarded: it lies roughly 85 km upstream and on the wrong side of the meridian.
stops.campa: Odo raises a second army and brings it back to the Garonne, and this one is destroyed. The sources are clear about the order: the field defeat outside Bordeaux, then the sack, then this. Exactly where on the river it happened is not recorded, and the site is placed near Bordeaux and no closer than that. Odo, beaten twice in a season and now without a duchy to raise a third army from, rides north to ask Charles Martel, mayor of the palace and the real power in Francia, for men.
stops.quote: He gave battle to Duke Eudes (of Aquitaine) beyond the Garonne and the Dordogne, and put him to flight---so utterly [was he beaten] that God alone knew the number of the slain and wounded.
stops.quote_source: Isidore of Beja's Chronicle (the Continuation of the Chronicle of 754), trans. William Stearns Davis, Readings in Ancient History, vol. 2; Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks Project
suggested_refs: The Battle of the River Garonne, 732, second and decisive defeat of Odo of Aquitaine
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours', on Odo's appeal to Charles Martel

stops.name: Angouleme, the road north
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No primary source names Angouleme in the 732 march. The waypoint is inferred from the Roman road between Bordeaux and Poitiers; the month is a placeholder between the Garonne and the approach to Poitiers.
stops.campa: The road from Bordeaux to Poitiers runs through Angouleme, and later accounts route the army through it. No primary source names the town. It is on this journey because the ground between two attested points has to be crossed by something, and the Roman roads are what there was to cross it on. Behind the column southern Gaul is being stripped; ahead of it, nobody in Aquitaine yet knows that a Frankish army is coming down from the north to meet it.
suggested_refs: The Roman road from Burdigala to Limonum, the Bordeaux to Poitiers axis
sources: Not named in the Chronicle of 754 or the Fredegar continuations: recorded as a geographic inference
Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours', on the devastation of southern Gaul

segments.name: The Road Between Poitiers and Tours

stops.name: Poitiers, the approach to the city
stops.date_confidence: attested for the army's path, inferred for the day. The Chronicle of 754 names Poitiers as within the line of advance; the calendar of the approach is reconstructed backward from the battle.
stops.campa: Poitiers is wealthy, walled, and full of churches, and it stands on the road to Tours. The Chronicle of 754 puts the army in its path. By now the column is slowed by everything it has taken: the baggage out of Bordeaux and the Garonne is an army's worth of plunder moving at the pace of an ox, guarded by men who consider it theirs. That train is the reason this campaign is still moving and it will be the reason the campaign ends. It is nine days from the field.
suggested_refs: Poitiers, on the Roman road north from Bordeaux toward Tours
sources: Wikipedia, 'Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi', on the baggage train

stops.name: Poitiers, the basilica of Saint-Hilaire
stops.date_confidence: contradictory. French Wikipedia states the site was devastated, first by the Muslims under Abdiraman in 732. A separate medieval hagiographic tradition holds the church was saved from burning by a miracle. The Chronicle of 754 records no episode at Poitiers at all. Three accounts, no reconciliation offered. The day is inferred.
stops.campa: Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand stands outside the walls. The French record says the site was devastated, first by the Muslims under Abdiraman in 732; a competing medieval hagiography says the church was spared by a miracle at the moment the army meant to fire it. The two stories are about the same building and they contradict each other flatly, and the near-contemporary chronicle mentions no episode here whatever. Charles Martel's own record of these events carries the burning as fact, dated to the tenth of October. The sources disagree with each other, and the disagreement stands here unresolved.
suggested_refs: The church of Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand, Poitiers, outside the walls on the northern road
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Eglise Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand de Poitiers' (devastated in 732)
Medieval Frankish hagiographic tradition of Saint Hilary (miraculous sparing)
charles_martel.journey.json ('Poitiers, Saint-Hilaire burned'), for the inherited pin and the internal disagreement

stops.name: Tours, the shrine of Saint Martin named as the prize
stops.date_confidence: attested as an objective, never reached. The Chronicle of 754 names the basilica of Saint Martin as what draws the raid north of Poitiers. The date marks the point in the campaign at which the objective is declared, not an arrival: al-Ghafiqi never enters Tours.
stops.campa: The shrine of Saint Martin at Tours is the richest treasury in Gaul, and the chronicle names it outright as what pulls the army north past Poitiers. Al-Ghafiqi never reaches it. This stop is an objective and not an arrival, the northernmost point the campaign aims at, pinned where Clovis heard the psalm sung in 507 and where Charles Martel will come in November to give thanks for the fact that nobody arrived. Seven hundred years later Jehanne d'Arc will be armed in this city.
stops.quote: Whereupon Abderrahman set in pursuit of Eudes; he destroyed palaces, burned churches, and imagined he could pillage the basilica of St. Martin of Tours.
stops.quote_source: Isidore of Beja's Chronicle (the Continuation of the Chronicle of 754), trans. William Stearns Davis, Readings in Ancient History, vol. 2; Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks Project
suggested_refs: The abbey and shrine of Saint Martin at Tours, treasury of Gaul and declared objective of the 732 raid
sources: charles_martel.journey.json, clovis.journey.json, joan_of_arc.journey.json, all pinned at Tours

stops.name: The Roman road, seven days of watching
stops.date_confidence: attested for the standoff, reconstruction for the point on the road. The Chronicle of 754 records almost seven days of mutual observation before the engagement. The coordinate is an approximate point on the Poitiers-Tours axis, not a located camp.
stops.campa: Charles Martel has come south with Franks, Gauls, and Germans, avoiding open ground where cavalry would own the day, and has put his army across the road on a wooded plateau. The two hosts come in sight of each other and stop. For nearly seven days they hold position and skirmish, each waiting for the other to commit first. The Arabic historians will name this road the balat al-shuhada, the pavement of the martyrs, and that name will outlive every other detail of the week, including the week's own date.
stops.quote: It is then that he found himself face to face with the lord of Austrasia, Charles, a mighty warrior from his youth, and trained in all the occasions of arms.
stops.quote_source: Isidore of Beja's Chronicle (the Continuation of the Chronicle of 754), trans. William Stearns Davis, Readings in Ancient History, vol. 2; Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks Project
suggested_refs: The Roman road between Poitiers and Tours, called in the Arabic sources the pavement of the martyrs
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours', on the seven days of skirmishing

stops.name: The field of Tours-Poitiers, the wall of ice
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle, contested for the day, unlocated for the field. English Wikipedia gives 10 October 732; Arabic Wikipedia gives 27 Sha'ban 114 AH, that is 21 October. The atlas's own charles_martel.journey.json dates the pitched battle 732-10-25. Three dates, none reconciled. The pin is inherited from charles_martel.journey.json and is a placeholder, not a located field.
stops.campa: The Frankish infantry forms a square on ground of its own choosing and does not move. The Umayyad cavalry charges it, and charges it again, and goes on charging it through the day. This is the wrong battle for the army that fought its way here from Pamplona: no room to work, no flank to turn, a formation that will not open. Charles Martel's own record places this field some seven kilometres south of where scholars now locate it, and both locations stand here rather than pretending to know which is the ground.
stops.quote: in the shock of the battle the men of the North seemed like a sea that cannot be moved. Firmly they stood, one close to another, forming as it were a bulwark of ice; and with great blows of their swords they hewed down the Arabs.
stops.quote_source: Isidore of Beja's Chronicle (the Continuation of the Chronicle of 754), trans. William Stearns Davis, Readings in Ancient History, vol. 2; Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks Project
suggested_refs: The field between Tours and Poitiers, 10 October 732
sources: charles_martel.journey.json ('The field of Tours-Poitiers, the wall of ice'), for the inherited pin

stops.name: The camp, the plunder defended
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Fredegar continuation describes the camp raid disrupting the Umayyad line, and the biography records that a portion of the force broke off to defend captured booty. The hour is not recorded.
stops.campa: A Frankish detachment gets in behind the line and into the Umayyad camp. What is in that camp is Bordeaux and the Garonne, four months of taking, along with the wives and the camp followers who have come the whole road from Pamplona. Men leave the fighting line to defend it. The report of a raid on the baggage travels through the ranks as a report of a retreat, and the charges that have been breaking on the square all day begin to come apart from behind instead of in front.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad baggage camp at the Tours-Poitiers field, holding the plunder of Aquitaine

stops.name: The field, the death of al-Ghafiqi
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death, contradictory for the manner. The Chronicle of 754 says the Austrasians found him and struck him on the chest; the Arabic tradition has him mortally wounded by an arrow while reordering the ranks. The pool's claim that both traditions agree he was rallying a retreat and was surrounded is corrected: the Latin source supplies neither detail.
stops.campa: Al-Ghafiqi rides into the disorder to hold his own men in place. The Arabic tradition has him mortally wounded by an arrow while reordering the ranks; the near-contemporary Latin chronicle says only that the people of Austrasia found him and struck him on the chest. The two accounts are usually welded into one heroic sentence about a commander dying to stop a rout, and they should not be. What both do agree on is that he is on the field when it turns and that he does not come off it.
stops.quote: The people of Austrasia, greater in a number of soldiers and formidably armed, killed the king, Abd ar-Rahman, when they found him, striking him on the chest.
stops.quote_source: Chronicle of 754 (the Mozarabic Chronicle), trans. Kenneth Baxter Wolf, Conquerors and Chroniclers of Early Medieval Spain, Translated Texts for Historians 9 (Liverpool University Press, 2nd ed. 1999), p. 145. Reached through multiple independent hosts citing this edition; Fordham's chron754.asp returned HTTP 500 and web.archive.org was unreachable from this environment, so the printed page was not opened directly.
suggested_refs: The Chronicle of 754, the nearest source in time to the battle, written in al-Andalus by a Christian a generation after
sources: Chronicle of 754, trans. Wolf, p. 145, via secondary hosts
Arabic Wikipedia, entry on al-Ghafiqi (the arrow)

stops.name: The camp abandoned in the night
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Fredegar continuation and the Chronicle of 754 both describe the silent night withdrawal and the Franks' cautious approach to the empty camp at dawn. The failure to agree on a successor commander is attributed to tribal and ethnic factionalism in the biography.
stops.campa: The army does not break that night. It decides. With the wali dead, the surviving commanders cannot settle which of them succeeds him, Arab against Berber, tribe against tribe, and rather than fight a second day under nobody they strike nothing and go. The tents are left standing. In the morning the Franks come at the camp expecting an ambush, walk into it, find it empty, and only then understand what they have. Nobody pursues. The road south is open all the way to the passes.
stops.quote: These spies discovered that all the squadrons of the "Ishmaelites" had vanished. In fact, during the night they had fled with the greatest silence, seeking with all speed their home land.
stops.quote_source: Isidore of Beja's Chronicle (the Continuation of the Chronicle of 754), trans. William Stearns Davis, Readings in Ancient History, vol. 2; Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks Project
suggested_refs: The abandoned Umayyad camp, morning of 11 October 732
sources: Wikipedia, 'Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi', on the factional failure to name a successor

stops.name: Moussais-la-Bataille, the field the scholars name
stops.date_confidence: modern identification, not attestation. English Wikipedia gives 46 degrees 46 minutes 52 seconds N, 0 degrees 32 minutes 26 seconds E for the battle and states that the exact location remains unclear from the surviving sources. The pool's 46.7167, 0.6167 is discarded: it lies about 7 km south and 6 km east, across the Vienne near Bonneuil-Matours.
stops.campa: Where the battle was actually fought is not recorded by anybody who was there. The name Poitiers attached to it early and Tours later; the ground itself was reasoned out by modern historians from toponymy and terrain and settled on the hamlet of Moussais, in the commune of Vouneuil-sur-Vienne, north of Poitiers on the Roman road. English Wikipedia still calls the exact location unclear from the surviving sources. Europe has been telling a founding story about this ground for thirteen centuries without agreeing which ground it is.
suggested_refs: Moussais-la-Bataille, commune of Vouneuil-sur-Vienne, the site now identified with the battle
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours' (coordinate and the caveat)

stops.name: Cordoba, the news of the defeat
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The succession of governors after 732 is documented; no source describes the news arriving in Cordoba, and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The news comes down the passes in pieces and reaches Cordoba before the winter closes: the army south of the mountains, the governor dead in Gaul. A successor is appointed and the province goes on. The frontier does not. Umayyad arms will hold Septimania another generation and raid north again more than once, but the line al-Ghafiqi reached in October is the farthest into western Europe the caliphate ever comes, and from Gibbon onward historians will hang the meaning of a century on that one afternoon.
stops.quote: The king Abdirama having been killed, he destroyed [them], driving forth the army, he fought and won.
stops.quote_source: Continuations of the Chronicle of Fredegar, ch. 13, as translated in Paul Fouracre, The Age of Charles Martel (Harlow: Longman, 2000), p. 149; Fouracre's rendering derives from J. M. Wallace-Hadrill, The Fourth Book of the Chronicle of Fredegar with its Continuations (1960). Verified across independent hosts citing this translation; the printed page was not opened in this pass.
suggested_refs: The succession of walis of al-Andalus after October 732
sources: Ibn Idhari, Al-Bayan al-Mughrib, on the succession
Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours', on the traditional framing of the limit of expansion

stops.name: The road between Poitiers and Tours, balat al-shuhada
stops.date_confidence: the naming tradition is Arabic and later; the date is a placeholder immediately after the battle, not an event date. No source dates the coining of the name.
stops.campa: In Arabic the battle keeps the name of the road it was fought beside: balat al-shuhada. Al-Ghafiqi is not a defeated general in that tradition, he is a martyr, and one of the greatest governors al-Andalus had. This is his afterlife and it is the only one he is given. There is no tomb. No source in Latin, French, or Arabic records where his body went, whether it was carried off the field, or whether any marker was ever raised over it anywhere. The gap is complete and it is left as a gap.
stops.quote: Abd ar-Rahman and many of his men found martyrdom on the balat ash-Shuhada'i (the path of the martyrs)
stops.quote_source: Antonio Santosuosso, Barbarians, Marauders, and Infidels: The Ways of Medieval Warfare (Boulder: Westview Press, 2004), p. 126, quoting Ibn Idhari al-Marrakushi. No edition or translation of al-Bayan al-Mughrib was reachable in this pass; every occurrence of this English wording traces to Santosuosso, so it is cited as his rendering and not as a direct translation from the thirteenth-century Arabic.
suggested_refs: The Arabic name of the battle, balat al-shuhada, preserved in the historiography of al-Andalus and the Maghreb
sources: Santosuosso, Barbarians, Marauders, and Infidels, p. 126
Burial place: absent from English, French, and Arabic sources alike, recorded as an absence

stops.name: Louchapt, the cliff of the Sangou
stops.date_confidence: legend, and dated only to the year 733 by the tradition itself. The month is a placeholder. The coordinate is approximate: French Wikipedia places Loupchat about 3 km from the town of Martel and gives no point of its own.
stops.campa: A tradition in the Haut-Quercy refuses the whole story. In this version al-Ghafiqi is not killed at Poitiers at all: he escapes south toward Narbonne, is overtaken by Charles Martel the following year, and dies at Louchapt at the foot of the Sangou cliff in 733. Nothing supports it. Pierre Riche has even proposed that the epithet Martel, the Hammer, was earned here rather than on the Tours road. It is kept because this is what the place itself remembers, and this stretch of the Lot remembers its own ending.
suggested_refs: The falaise du Sangou and the locality of Louchapt or Loupchat, Lot, France

stops.name: Narbonne, the last Umayyad city in Gaul
stops.date_confidence: attested. The pool's 'until the 750s' is corrected: Pepin the Short began the siege of Narbonne in 752, but the city did not fall until 759, so Umayyad Septimania outlived al-Ghafiqi by twenty-seven years.
stops.campa: The defeat on the Poitiers road does not end the Umayyad hold on Gaul. Narbonne, the base al-Ghafiqi marched out of in 721 and the garrison the survivors of 732 fell back through, stays in Muslim hands for another twenty-seven years. Charles Martel besieges it in 737 and fails; Pepin the Short begins a siege in 752 and takes the city only in 759, a generation after the man who last led an army north from it was struck on the chest in a field he never named.
suggested_refs: Narbonne, held by the Umayyads from 719 until its fall to Pepin the Short in 759
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours', on the continued Umayyad hold on Septimania
charles_martel.journey.json ('Narbonne, the siege on the Aude', 737), for the inherited pin

stops.name: Martel in the Lot, the town that took the name
stops.date_confidence: attested for the documentary record, legendary for the foundation story. The first documented mention of the town is in the cartulary of Aubazine, 1142; the settlement grew in the eleventh century around a salt market. No manuscript links Charles Martel to the place before the sixteenth century.
stops.campa: Three kilometres from the cliff stands the town of Martel, which says Charles Martel founded it to mark a victory over the Saracens. Its own history takes the claim apart: first documented mention in the cartulary of Aubazine in 1142, a settlement grown in the eleventh century around a salt market, and no manuscript linking Charles Martel to the ground before the sixteenth. Its arms carry hammers and it calls itself the town of seven towers. The name arrived first and the story came looking for it afterward.
suggested_refs: Martel, Lot, the ville aux sept tours, and its arms bearing hammers
sources: The pool's 'seven anvils' is corrected here: the town's designation is seven towers, and the arms bear hammers

stops.name: Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, the sword behind the altar
stops.date_confidence: legendary for the deposit, attested for the retrieval. The votive burial of Charles Martel's sword is tradition carried in charles_martel.journey.json; the 1429 letter and the finding of a sword behind the altar belong to the documented record of Jehanne d'Arc. The atlas's two journeys pin the chapel 500 m apart, 47.152 and 47.157; this stop takes the Charles Martel value because the chain begins there.
stops.campa: The story that grew out of the victory kept growing. Charles Martel, riding south from Tours, is said to have buried his sword behind the altar of the chapel here as a votive offering for the defeat of al-Ghafiqi. Seven hundred years later Jehanne d'Arc, who has never been inside the building, sends a letter from Tours asking for a sword she says is buried behind that altar, and the armourers dig and find one. The death on the Poitiers road is the first link in a chain that ends at Orleans.
suggested_refs: The chapel of Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, between Tours and Poitiers on the pilgrim road
sources: charles_martel.journey.json ('Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, the sword left behind the altar')

stops.name: Paris, the bronze in the Louvre
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the cast. The Steuben painting mentioned in the campa is dated 1837 by English Wikipedia; French Wikipedia carries the Gechter bronze and its Louvre location.
stops.campa: Theodore Gechter casts a bronze group in 1833 and titles it the combat of Charles Martel and Abd al-Rahman, king of the Saracens; it enters the Louvre. Four years later Charles de Steuben finishes a history painting of the battle on the scale France reserved that decade for the founding of nations. Al-Ghafiqi is in both, mounted, at the moment of losing. A man of whom no source records a face, a birth year, or a grave is kept in French bronze and French oil because of the one afternoon he was killed.
suggested_refs: Theodore Gechter, Le combat de Charles Martel et d'Abd al-Rahman, roi des Sarrasins, bronze, 1833, Musee du Louvre
Charles de Steuben, Bataille de Poitiers, 1837
